The technical challenge that arises when applying Art. 50 II watermarking to synthetic data used for AI training is that watermarks designed to be human-readable can interfere with the training process, as AI systems may learn to recognize these watermarks as features relevant to the training data rather than disregarding them. This jeopardizes the integrity of the training data, creating a conflict between the regulatory requirement for persistent labeling and the technical need for clean data in model training pipelines.

In comparison, fact-checking systems face a different marking challenge. The iterative nature of editorial workflows in journalism leads to the fragility of text watermarking techniques, as the human review process can destroy the marks embedded in AI-generated content. Unlike synthetic data, where a dual-version solution can separate marked and unmarked outputs, fact-checking systems do not have an equivalent separation point, making it difficult to maintain the provenance of AI-generated outputs once they are edited by humans. Thus, while both cases deal with the fragility of watermarks, the specific operational contexts and challenges differ significantly.
